k1.text: For a drawer front, start with a 1/4-inch or 3/8-inch screw, depending on how thick the wood is. If the screw head will show, use a countersink bit so it sits flush or just below the surface. That keeps it neat without making the joint look messy.

If you already have a drill, check whether it has a countersink bit or a small pilot bit. A pilot bit helps make the hole straight, and a countersink bit makes the screw head sit lower. If not, a small hand drill bit can still work for a quick test.

That’s fine. If you can’t find a countersink bit, just drill the hole first, then use a small screwdriver to tap the screw in by hand. If the screw starts to slip, stop and make the hole a little shallower before trying again.
Yes, that’s the safest order. Glue the joint first, clamp it, and let it dry fully before adding the screw. If the joint stays loose after that, then the screw is the next step.
Good plan. If you run into any trouble, feel free to ask for help with the exact steps.

k2.text: If you already have a drill, check whether it has a countersink bit or a small pilot bit. A pilot bit helps make the hole straight, and a countersink bit makes the screw head sit lower. If not, a small hand drill bit can still work, but it may leave a rough edge.

That’s a good idea. A hand drill is easier than a power drill for this job, especially if the piece is old and delicate. If you want, I can walk you through the steps in order so you can ask him exactly what he needs to do.

Yes, that’s the safest order. Try the glue and clamps first, then add the screw only if the joint still feels loose after it dries. If the glue joint is weak, the screw can act as a backup without making the whole thing look messy.
Good plan. If you run into any trouble, feel free to describe the exact setup and I’ll help you troubleshoot it step by step.

k1.text: Exactly. Even pressure usually flattens the picture, while selective darkening creates shape. If you want, I can also help you pick which shadow to deepen first so the whole still life feels more believable.

That’s a useful angle. In still lifes, sharp edges often look too clean, while soft edges can make the form feel flat. A mix of both, controlled by distance from the light source, usually works better than one hard line across the whole piece.
Good plan. If you want, send me a quick photo of the still life and I can help you spot the exact spots that need more contrast or softer edges.
That’s a common trap. Highlights should be bright, yes, but they also need to stay small and specific, otherwise they can pull attention away from the form.

No problem at all. If you want, I can give you a very short checklist for the next round: 1) compare light and dark values, 2) soften the edges near the tablecloth, 3) keep highlights small, 4) test one area at a time.
Yes, that sounds like a good move. A little fresh air can clear your head and make the still life feel less tense. If you come back with a photo later, I’d be happy to help you read it.
That would be a nice thing to include. Roses can add a lot of color and texture, and they’re great for testing how light changes across petals and stems.

Absolutely. Natural scenes often show the same principles more clearly than a still life, so it’s a good way to check your thinking. If you want, I can also help you notice the same contrasts when you come back inside.

k1.text: Probably, yes. A simple memory trick can feel like a small magic trick when it works well. If you want, I can make it sound more like a game than a lesson.

k1.text: For tomatoes, a few inches between each plant is usually enough, depending on the variety. If you’re moving them outside, keep them in a sheltered spot at first and watch for wind, since strong gusts can bend the stems even more.
Yes, that’s a good thing to check. If there’s a chance of wind, you can also tie the stems loosely to the cage with soft string or strips of cloth so they don’t snap.

A larger cage is usually better if you can fit it. It gives the plant more room to grow without needing constant adjustment, and that can help prevent the stems from getting weak. If space is tight, you can still use a smaller cage and just give the plants a little more support overall.
Absolutely. Measure the space once, then choose the cage based on that, so you’re not fighting the layout later. If you tell me the patio width and depth, I can help you estimate the best cage size.

Not much for tomatoes, no. Wire, plastic, or even bamboo can work well, as long as it’s sturdy enough to hold the plant upright. The main thing is that it’s open enough for air to circulate and not too heavy to move if needed.

Absolutely. Measure the space, then choose a cage that fits comfortably after the plants are in it. That way you won’t be stuck trying to squeeze something that’s too big later.
